Each fold of the data judges the update chosen on the other folds (cross-fitting) to reduce selection bias; acceptance requires the gain's lower bootstrap bound to exceed a margin. The false-improvement rate falls from 19.1% (naive) to 1.1% (BRIDGE) in (A), 20.7% to 1.7% (B), 20.0% to 0% (C), and 12.5% to 0.5% (D); every 95% confidence interval of the reduction over datasets or tasks excludes zero (not over the clinical sources). An equal-size random draw from the naive acceptances contains more false improvements in (A)-(E) (post hoc, p<0.001). On the OpenML collection (E) of 14 new datasets, the false-improvement rate falls from 25.6% to 1.0%. BRIDGE removes 97% to 100% of the false improvements that the naive rule accepts, and its mean gain per deployed update is 1.8 to 3.1 times the naive rule's. papers.title: Temporal difference learning adapts to incomplete coverage: an oracle inequality over subgraphs
papers.summary: Temporal difference (TD) and Monte Carlo (MC) are two fundamental principles for value function estimation in reinforcement learning. papers.title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation

papers.title: Finite-Sample Sensitivity of Kernel Metrics for Generative Evaluation
papers.summary: Kernel distances such as the Kernel Inception Distance (KID) and the Kernel Audio Distance (KAD) compare generated and reference samples in an embedding space, and model comparisons rest on their values. Each ships with one fixed kernel, and a reported value does not say which changes that kernel detects at the sample size used. We run each default as a permutation two-sample test on real embeddings of symbolic music, audio and images, comparing a sample with an independent sample changed by a mean shift, an isotropic contraction, or a rotation that keeps the mean and the covariance trace and is matched to the shift in transport distance. At 780 samples per side, both defaults rarely detect the rotations in five evaluation spaces, while they detect the shifts in every run. The median-bandwidth Gaussian kernel of KAD detects the contraction and regains power against rotations on image embeddings with an order of magnitude more samples. The cubic kernel of KID contains second- and third-moment information but misses the contraction in most runs, and our experiments do not establish a high-power rotation regime for it over the tested sample sizes. Narrower Gaussian bandwidths restore sensitivity in music and audio, an $\ell_1$ Laplace kernel does so for images, and aggregated tests combine both at nominal level. We recommend that a reported kernel distance state its sample budget and the changes its configuration detects at that budget.

papers.title: Machine learning kinetics from molecular dynamics data
papers.summary: Most molecular transitions occur on time scales far beyond direct molecular dynamics simulations. The committor, the probability that a configuration reaches a product state before a reactant state, is a central kinetic statistic, providing a mechanism-independent reaction coordinate and a foundation for transition path theory and the calculation of rates. We conclude by identifying opportunities for further research, including connections to reinforcement learning and generative modeling.

papers.summary: One of the fundamental differences between biological neural networks and artificial neural networks (ANNs) is that biological neurons obey Dale's principle: each neuron projects either exclusively excitatory or exclusively inhibitory outputs. papers.title: Ranking Is Not Deciding: Benchmark Shortcuts and Operating-Point Collapse in Query-Time RAG Poisoning Defenses

papers.title: NEOPIC: A Neural Operator Framework for Particle-based Kinetic Plasma Simulations
papers.summary: We introduce NEOPIC, a framework for learning the field operator in particle-based methods applied to kinetic plasma simulations. papers.title: Zero-Complement Extrapolation: Parameter Recovery and Classification in Severely Imbalanced Logistic Regression under Rank-Deficient Regimes
papers.summary: Parameter estimation and classification in binary logistic regression deteriorate severely when the number of minority class observations ($n_1$) is smaller than the feature dimension ($p$). We further establish that extrapolating synthetic minority instances outward from the high-quantile density fringe of the majority distribution along the conjugate direction preserves full-rank covariance regularity ($\mathrm{rank} = p$). papers.title: Data Schedules and Learning Rate Schedules Should Be Designed Together

papers.title: Self-Organizing Maps with Optimized Latent Positions
papers.summary: Self-Organizing Maps (SOM) are a classical method for unsupervised learning, vector quantization, and topographic mapping of high-dimensional data. However, existing SOM formulations often involve a trade-off between computational efficiency and a clearly defined optimization objective. Objective-based variants such as Soft Topographic Vector Quantization (STVQ) provide a principled formulation, but their neighborhood-coupled computations become expensive as the number of latent nodes increases. In this paper, we propose Self-Organizing Maps with Optimized Latent Positions (SOM-OLP), an objective-based topographic mapping method that introduces a continuous latent position for each data point. Starting from the neighborhood distortion of STVQ, we construct a separable surrogate local cost based on its local quadratic structure and formulate an entropy-regularized objective based on it. This yields a simple block coordinate descent scheme with closed-form updates for assignment probabilities, latent positions, and reference vectors, while guaranteeing monotonic non-increase of the objective and retaining linear per-iteration complexity in the numbers of data points and latent nodes. Experiments on a synthetic saddle manifold, scalability studies on the Digits and MNIST datasets, and 16 benchmark datasets show that SOM-OLP achieves competitive neighborhood preservation and quantization performance, favorable scalability for large numbers of latent nodes and large datasets, and the best average rank among the compared methods on the benchmark datasets.

papers.title: A Gradient based Adversarial Augmentation Framework for Mitigating Unlearnable Datasets
papers.summary: Unlearnable data methods (ULD) protect public data from unauthorized model training by adding imperceptible perturbations that create a learning shortcut. A deep neural network can exploit the shortcut learning path to minimize training loss without learning generalizable features. Intuitively, finding adversarial versions of perturbed images that can substantially increase the model's loss can force the model to learn generalizable features. Existing data augmentation based attacks rely on heuristic search strategies/random sampling over a curated augmentation set to identify adversarial augmentation operations, an approach that often does not scale when the number of candidate operations is large. To address the challenge of a large search space, we propose {\techname}, a gradient based adversarial augmentation framework that learns an augmentation policy via stochastic gradient ascent. {\techname} leverages a differentiable data augmentation pipeline to efficiently search a set of up to 18 augmentation techniques, from which a grid search selects a protection-specific subset. The augmentation subset is trained to maximize a surrogate model's classification loss. We introduce a perceptual-plus-pixel regularization to learn operation parameters that preserve image semantics. Under a controlled ablation, {\techname} consistently outperforms an equivalent random sampling baseline (80.0\% vs. 77.29\% clean test accuracy on EMIN-protected CIFAR-10 for ResNet-18 and 83.28\% vs. 66.45\% on NTGA-protected CIFAR-10 for MobileNet-V2), demonstrating that gradient guidance drives the clean test accuracy recoverability rather than the expanded search space. {\techname} offers an effective and scalable adversarial augmentation framework for stress-testing ULD methods, a critical tool for developing robust ULD methods.

papers.title: On Worst-Case Guarantees for Graph-Based Nearest-Neighbor Search
papers.summary: Graph-based nearest neighbor search algorithms like HNSW, DiskANN, NSG, and others have surged in popularity in recent years due to their excellent empirical performance in comparison to space-partitioning methods like IVF data structures and Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH). However, in contrast to LSH and related methods, obtaining strong worst-case theoretical guarantees for graph-based search has proven challenging. In this paper, we prove a strong lower bound that helps explain the lack of progress towards such guarantees. We show that no standard graph-based method (any that runs a variant of greedy search on a flat or hierarchical graph) can achieve sublinear query time for approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space, even for an arbitrarily large approximation factor. On the other hand, we prove that sublinear query time is possible if we allow for Steiner points in the search graph. We obtain bounds comparable to LSH, showing e.g., that graph-based search with Steiner points can solve $c$-approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space with query time $\tilde{O}(n^{1/(c-1)})$. We complement this result with initial experiments exploring how Steiner points can be incorporated into practical graph-based methods.

papers.title: What Does LOL Measure? Hidden Label Shifts in Low-Light Enhancement Benchmarks
papers.summary: LOL-v1 and LOLv2-Real are the standard benchmarks for supervised low-light image enhancement, and several leading methods ship hand-set test-time adjustments with their evaluation scripts. (i) The 15 LOL-v1 test labels are rendered differently: the same captures appear in LOLv2 with labels of identical luminance but 1.48x lower saturation, and LOL-v1's own training labels match the LOLv2 rendering; we confirm this on the official release. (ii) The LOLv2-Real test set is the contiguous block of images 690-789, whose labels are 14% darker than the training labels (Cliff's delta = -0.45, p < 1e-12) with no comparable shift in the input statistics we examined; methods trained without any labels score up to 5.5 dB higher on test than on train. (iii) All 15 LOL-v1 test inputs reappear in LOLv2-Real, 12 in its training set. The released test-time settings are consistent with compensating for these shifts. Separating what can be calibrated on training data from what only test-set tuning finds, the test-only residual has median 0.00 dB on LOLv2-Syn, which has no shift, but 0.37 dB on LOL-v1 and 0.92 dB on LOLv2-Real (up to 3.9 dB). Under the shift, test-set checkpoint selection inflates a from-scratch model by 0.9-2.0 dB, and removing the released settings changes which method ranks first. papers.title: CADENCE: Distributional Next-Transaction Forecasting for Business Cash-Flow Underwriting
papers.summary: Recurring cash flows are the backbone of cash-flow underwriting: they separate durable revenue from one-off deposits, expose standing obligations, and ultimately determine ability to pay. papers.title: Robust and efficient enriched representation with intrinsic neuronal heterogeneity
papers.summary: Heterogeneity is a ubiquitous property of many biological systems with profound computational implications. We suggest that, despite being task-agnostic, heterogeneity enhances representational capacity by diversifying neuronal responses, demonstrated on two machine-learning and one neuroscience benchmark. Our work highlights the utility of intrinsic task-agnostic heterogeneity for versatile, energy-efficient computing--a highly relevant property for the neuromorphic community, where device-to-device variability could be exploited to offset limited training budgets and architectural constraints.

papers.title: FunnelAL: Retrieve-then-Rank Active Learning for Single-Class Discovery

papers.title: Twincher: Towards Robust and Precise Physical AI via Bijective Representation Learning
papers.summary: Perception and planning in physical systems often require inverting a continuous forward map $p \mapsto y = f(p)$, e.g., a renderer or a simulator, that can be queried but not inverted in closed form. Learned inverses are limited by their approximation error, whereas iterative solvers in observation space can stall at spurious stationary points. We instead learn a representation $r(y)$, insensitive to perturbations of $y$ normal to the data manifold, in which $p \mapsto r(f(p))$ is a well-conditioned bijection. In these coordinates, the least-squares inverse problem has no spurious interior stationary points, so that Gauss-Newton iteration with the exact forward model converges to the accuracy the data permit; the learned model need only be qualitatively correct. We introduce Twincher, an exactly invertible architecture of localized area-preserving rotations, trained with Jacobian-level objectives and a domain-growing curriculum. On synthetic maps with tunable nonconvexity, the worst-case residual reaches machine precision within five iterations once the query budget suffices, whereas an MLP-based baseline improves only gradually. In 6D localization of industrial objects in real depth images of the MVTec ITODD benchmark, given instance masks, twinchers trained only on CAD renderings make the iteration converge from a fixed initial guess within a few steps, without feature matching, pose regression, or pose hypotheses; in observation space, the same iteration fails for up to half of the views. papers.title: When Visual Evidence Is Insufficient: How Instructions, Post-Training, and Internal Activations Shape Refusal in Multimodal Language Models

papers.title: An end-to-end framework for uncertainty-aware validation of generative models
papers.summary: Density estimation with generative models is a common task in the physical sciences, for example in background estimation in particle physics. Existing machine learning techniques, however, lack methods to quantify uncertainties that can be propagated into a statistical test. But a model fitted to a finite training set is never exact, so if its uncertainties are neglected, any sufficiently powerful goodness-of-fit test will eventually reject it once the test set is large enough to resolve this estimation error. We use Gaussian mixture models, for which uncertainties are tractable, and further construct a new goodness-of-fit test in which these uncertainties are profiled as nuisance parameters to account for the statistical error of the fit, promoting the conventional point-null test to a composite one. A rejection then signals genuine mismodeling rather than a test set large enough to resolve the error of the fit, provided the propagated uncertainties faithfully cover that error. We demonstrate the framework on a controlled two-dimensional toy model and on a collider physics benchmark modeling the QCD background process. With uncertainties included, the same model can be trusted on test sets up to an order of magnitude larger than the standard test allows. Our work thus provides a statistically grounded basis for a robust use of generative models in the physical sciences.

papers.title: LinMix: Data Mixing as Linear Domain Attribution

papers.title: Sharpness-Aware Muon: Matrix-Aware Optimization with Momentum-Guided Perturbations

papers.title: Maestro: Agentic Formal Proof Development by Coordination
papers.summary: Lean is increasingly used to verify mathematical proofs and software produced by LLM agents, but writing formal proofs remains hard. Existing prover systems take a divide-and-conquer approach that recursively decomposes hard proof goals into easier lemmas and splits again any lemma that resists proof. Existing systems cannot tell these apart as a failed attempt reports little beyond its failure, and responses are confined to the failing node without considering the rest of the proof or revising the plan above it. The system may thus keep decomposing obligations along a flawed proof direction until the budget runs out, causing the whole proof attempt to fail. Provers report why they failed, not just that they failed, and a coordinator that sees the whole proof chooses an appropriate response, such as guiding a stuck prover, correcting a false lemma, or retracting a flawed subtree and replanning it. The same harness extends to verified code synthesis, where a checked counterexample sends the code back for repair. We evaluate Maestro with four frontier LLMs on seven mathematics and three software verification benchmarks. It proves more targets than each model's native coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) on every benchmark the agent has not already saturated, with the largest gains on research-level mathematics. papers.title: Anomaly Detection via Autoencoder Composite Features and NCE
papers.summary: Unsupervised anomaly detection is a challenging task. Autoencoders (AEs) or generative models are often employed to model the data distribution of normal inputs and subsequently identify anomalous, out-of-distribution inputs by high reconstruction error or low likelihood, respectively. However, AEs may generalize and achieve small reconstruction errors on abnormal inputs. We propose a decoupled training approach for anomaly detection that both an AE and a likelihood model trained with noise contrastive estimation (NCE). After training the AE, NCE estimates a probability density function, to serve as the anomaly score, on the joint space of the AE's latent representation combined with features of the reconstruction quality. To further reduce the false negative rate in NCE we systematically varying the reconstruction features to augment the training and optimize the contrastive Gaussian noise distribution. Experimental assessments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach matches the performance of prevalent state-of-the-art anomaly detection algorithms.

papers.title: High-Fidelity Aerostructural Dataset of Transonic Wings in Cruise Conditions
papers.summary: Recent advances in machine learning (ML) have the potential to substantially accelerate aircraft wing design, a process that has traditionally required extensive high-fidelity simulation and design iteration. Existing public datasets for ML-based wing design have focused primarily on aerodynamic performance, with limited consideration of the multidisciplinary interactions that govern practical aircraft design. In particular, efficient wing design requires simultaneous consideration of aerodynamic performance and structural integrity, yet no publicly available datasets capture this coupled aerostructural behavior at high-fidelity. To address this need, a high-fidelity multidisciplinary dataset for static aerostructural analysis of transonic wings is introduced. The dataset includes 2471 samples, along with three out-of-distribution samples. The wing planform geometry is parameterized by span, sweep, dihedral, tip chord, and tip twist, while the airfoil cross-sections are parameterized using the class-shape transformation method. The analysis is further parameterized by Mach number, angle of attack, altitude, and structural load factor. The utility of the dataset is demonstrated by training state-of-the-art ML models to predict aerodynamic surface quantities, integrated aerodynamic performance quantities, and the failure distribution of the wingbox. ML models achieve at most 0.0309 normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE) in the prediction of aerodynamic quantities and at most 0.1189 NRMSE in the prediction of failure distribution of the wingbox. By providing coupled aerodynamic and structural responses for a diverse set of transonic wings, this dataset establishes a benchmark for developing, evaluating, and comparing multi-physics ML models for wing design. Broadly, it is intended to encourage creation of similar high-fidelity multi-physics benchmark datasets across engineering domains.

papers.title: Compliance Moral Hazard and the Backfiring Mandate
papers.summary: Competing firms that share a population of risky customers face a decentralized risk detection problem in which each firm holds fragmentary information whose aggregation would generate social value, but private incentives impede truthful sharing. We develop a dynamic mechanism design framework for this setting and identify three strategic frictions that distinguish it from classical mechanism design with decentralized information: compliance moral hazard, adversarial adaptation, and information destruction through intervention. A temporal value assignment (TVA) mechanism credits firms using a strictly proper scoring rule applied to discounted verified outcomes; under stated assumptions, TVA implements truthful posterior reporting as a Bayes--Nash equilibrium (uniquely optimal at each edge in large federations, with $O(1/m)$ shading in finite systems). A network Shapley characterization shows that under edge-additive coalition value, each firm's marginal contribution is proportional to its weighted cross-firm interaction degree, yielding a sharp prescription for coalition design that prioritizes inter-firm volume over firm size. Embedding TVA in a model of competition among firms, we establish a welfare ordering across four regulatory regimes (autarky, voluntary federation, mandated full sharing, TVA) and identify conditions under which information-sharing mandates without compatible incentive design reduce welfare below autarky: a ``backfiring mandate.'' We illustrate the framework on a 1.4M-transaction synthetic anti-money-laundering benchmark; the same machinery extends to platform fraud, cybersecurity threat intelligence, and supply chain risk detection.

papers.title: ORBITAL: Optimization of Robust Brain--Computer Inference Through Architecture-Aware Low-Precision Compression

papers.title: Evaluating Federated Vision-Language and Vision-Only Models for Privacy-Aware Breast Cancer Imaging
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) shows promise for breast imaging, but limited labeled data, institutional data fragmentation, and privacy concerns hinder centralized training. We investigate a privacy-aware federated learning framework combining pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with client-level differential privacy. We compare general-purpose CLIP models, biomedical BiomedCLIP, and an ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 baseline on two public breast imaging datasets, with and without differential privacy. We also evaluate a CLIP ViT-B/16 ablation that removes the text pathway. Evaluation includes patient-level ROC-AUC with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, baseline comparisons, threshold sensitivity, inter-model agreement, and communication cost. Under federated learning, all five models achieve high normal-versus-sick discrimination (ROC-AUC: 0.940-0.990). However, acquisition year alone achieves 0.974 on the same test partition, raising concerns about confounding rather than genuine pathology recognition. Benign-versus-malignant discrimination remains uncertain (ROC-AUC: 0.504-0.637), with all confidence intervals including 0.50. Removing the text pathway preserves classification accuracy while halving communication cost. Differential privacy reduces ROC-AUC by 0.375, attributable to perturbing the full model state rather than only trainable parameters. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating confounding, predictive reliability, privacy implementation, and deployment efficiency when developing federated AI systems for breast imaging.

papers.title: Re-evaluating Confidence Remasking in Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.summary: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) have recently emerged as a competitive alternative to autoregressive language models, with the promise of faster inference via parallel token generation. A notable limitation of the masked formulation, however, is that once a token has been unmasked it can no longer be revised, leaving dLLMs vulnerable to early sampling mistakes. Confidence-based remasking methods aim to address this in a training-free manner by revising low-confidence tokens, with encouraging early results. In this work, we compare the accuracy-compute Pareto frontiers of three such methods (WINO, Saber, and COVER) to those of confidence-based unmasking alone (Fast-dLLM). We find that under greedy decoding, all three perform on par with Fast-dLLM at commonly used shorter block lengths; gains of remasking appear only at longer block lengths, where confidence-based unmasking is known to degrade. Under stochastic decoding, WINO reduces generation diversity beyond that of unmasking alone, while it helps recover from errors introduced by learned Bernoulli unmasking policies. Our results show that the benefits of confidence-based remasking are highly setting-dependent, underscoring the need for more comprehensive evaluation. Finally, our analyses point to the dLLM, not the remasking rule, as the bottleneck, suggesting that effective remasking may require changes to training, not only to inference.

papers.title: IOSage: Detecting HPC I/O Bottleneck Patterns to Guide LLM Recommendations
papers.summary: HPC applications often leave much of their parallel file system's bandwidth unused, and turning their Darshan logs into concrete I/O fixes still requires a scarce I/O expert. Rule-based tools flag counters against thresholds set by experts, and in tools built on large language models (LLMs), such as ION and IOAgent, the LLM decides which bottlenecks a log contains. We present IOSage, in which a classifier trained on many labeled logs, not the LLM, makes that decision, since a single log gives an LLM no baseline for what is abnormal. The LLM receives the I/O bottleneck patterns the classifier detects, the job's configuration files, per-file Darshan evidence, and for each pattern a card built from benchmark training runs, and writes recommended changes. Applied by hand and measured in repeated paired runs, the changes IOSage names speed up median total wall time 4.38x for an openPMD kernel (4.02x on a second storage tier) and 1.42x for hourly WRF restarts. For 5 of the 6 application scenarios with a helpful change, IOSage with Claude Sonnet 4 names it, including the change for 10-minute WRF restarts (up to 1.93x faster); with GPT-4o and Llama 3.1 as well, the classifier and cards name more helpful changes than the LLM alone. On 78 benchmark test runs without a pattern, the LLM deciding alone proposes changes for 64; with the classifier, for 9. The classifier reaches 0.929 Micro-F1 on 488 labeled benchmark test runs (0.916 as the gate; 0.832 on the 158 from configurations and jobs outside training), above Drishti's rules, WisIO, and IOAgent's pipeline without its literature retrieval. On TraceBench's nine expert-labeled traces from production systems, it has the highest precision of the tools compared (0.82), with 2 false positives against 12 for the keyword-mapped LLM diagnoses shipped with TraceBench and 5 for Drishti, on the five issue labels that match registered patterns.

papers.title: HELICS: Biobank-scale Conditional Synthetic Genome Generation via Latent Flow Matching
papers.summary: Individual-level genotype data underpin genetic discovery, disease-risk modeling, and therapeutic development, yet many critical settings remain data-limited, including underrepresented ancestries, rare or imbalanced disease cohorts, and restricted-access biobanks. We introduce HELICS: High-fidelity gEneration via Latent Interpolant Conditional Synthesis, a phasing-free latent flow matching framework for genome-wide SNP-level generation from biobank-scale genotype data. HELICS tokenizes chromosomes with convolutional autoencoders, reducing >600K SNPs to 4,096 continuous latent tokens, and trains a transformer parameterized conditional flow matching model over the concatenated multi-chromosome latent representation. Trained on over 417K genomes in the UK Biobank, HELICS generates genome-wide common-variant synthetic cohorts without haplotype phasing and achieves stronger fidelity to real genotypes than existing haplotype-based simulators, including high allele-frequency agreement in external evaluation and superior preservation of local and long-range SNP correlation structure. Conditioning on ancestry and genetic liability summaries enables targeted generation across genetic risk profiles; in perturbation analyses, by increasing the conditioned disease trait liability, HELICS induces SNP-level dosage changes in generated genomes that are highly correlated with published association weights. HELICS provides a scalable generative modeling framework for SNP-level genome data and a path toward conditional synthetic cohorts for data-limited genetic studies.

papers.title: Latent Nonlinear Denoising Score Matching for Enhanced Learning of Structured Distributions
papers.summary: Score-based generative models commonly employ linear forward diffusions with Gaussian reference distributions, limiting their ability to directly incorporate structural information into the noising dynamics. We introduce latent nonlinear denoising score matching (LNDSM), which combines nonlinear, structure-informed latent diffusions with the variational autoencoder (VAE) training framework. In our construction, the forward diffusion is designed to admit a prescribed reference distribution, such as a Gaussian mixture model, that reflects qualitative features of the latent data distribution. We derive a computable approximation to a cross-entropy upper bound in the VAE objective using Euler-Maruyama discretization and the resulting Gaussian conditional transitions. To stabilize training, we remove two zero-mean control variates whose variances become large for small time steps. The resulting objective enables joint training of the encoder, decoder, and latent score network. Numerical experiments on benchmark image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of LNDSM in learning structured distributions, outperforming conventional latent score-based generative modeling in sample quality and mode balance across several settings, while achieving improved training efficiency. These results highlight the potential of nonlinear, structure-informed latent diffusions for generative modeling.

papers.title: Beyond Update Counts: A Control Map for Evaluating Test-Time Model Updates
papers.summary: Test-time updating lets a language model change persistent state after training---such as model weights, adapter parameters, or a memory module---before or while answering queries. Existing evaluations often compare systems using update count or frequency and performance measured immediately afterward. These summaries omit what is updated, where, when, and in what order. The same total can therefore hide an important difference: one system may answer after one update while another answers after two. We introduce the Control Map, an evaluation framework that records the committed updates preceding each scored answer and separately evaluates behavioral changes, immediate learning (acquisition), later recall (retention), preservation of unrelated behavior (locality), and performance in new settings. We prove when counts alone determine final state and show, under stated assumptions, how differences between pre-answer histories limit differences in average scores. Using ControlMap, our experiments reveal three insights. First, update scheduling matters: at a 760M-parameter checkpoint, 24 schedules with the same update count yield 19.7%--34.2% accuracy. Second, learning an edit does not guarantee that it lasts or remains contained: all six selected CounterFact LoRA settings learn the new information, while ROME retains edits at all 13 operating points but fails locality at each. Third, no editor performs best consistently across models, benchmarks, and tests. Evaluations should therefore report update histories and assess acquisition, retention, and locality separately.

papers.title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
papers.summary: As foundation models evolve from information generation to digital work execution, agents are increasingly capable of completing complex tasks across tools, applications, and workflows. However, existing research lacks a unified perspective on how agents reliably accomplish delegated work. To address this gap, we present a work-centric, system-level perspective that views work agents as systems combining foundation models and runtime harnesses to execute tasks in stateful workspaces and deliver verifiable outcomes. We introduce two complementary dimensions, work persistence and work openness, to characterize working conditions, and classify digital work into five forms according to task scope and organization. Building on this framework, we identify five core capability families required for reliable work execution and examine approaches to model optimization, harness optimization, and their joint optimization. We further analyze existing evaluation methods and metrics from the perspective of work outcomes. Finally, we discuss future research directions, including sustained work delegation, adaptation to open environments, and the interaction between work execution and capability improvement. This paper provides a unified framework for understanding, optimizing, and evaluating work agents, supporting the development of systems capable of delivering reliable, verifiable, and practically valuable work outcomes.

papers.title: Does VGGT Know What It Does Not Know?
papers.summary: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models such as VGGT regress cameras and geometry in a single forward pass, but they report no uncertainty for the camera poses they predict: an incorrect relative pose looks no different from a correct one. We ask whether the frozen model nonetheless knows when its pose is wrong. On HardMatch, a benchmark of 1,000 deliberately difficult image pairs on which VGGT fails on 35% of pairs, a linear probe on VGGT's frozen features predicts pose failure on held-out categories with ROC-AUC 93.5%, compared with 79.7% for VGGT's own point-map confidence and 77.7% for a classifier trained on all of VGGT's outputs. The probe catches failures VGGT is confident about, lets a downstream system abstain on the pairs it distrusts, and transfers without retraining to rotation failures on PhotoTourism and ScanNet-1500, beyond what co-visibility explains. This knowledge is absent from the per-image encoder: it is computed partway through the layers that fuse the two views, and the same holds for a second model, $π^3$. In essence, we find that VGGT knows more about its own failures than it reports.

papers.title: CrystalREPA: Transferring Physical Priors from Universal MLIPs to Crystal Generative Models
papers.summary: Crystal generative models mainly learn what stable crystals look like, with little explicit supervision for what makes them stable. We reveal a substantial representation gap between state-of-the-art crystal generative models and pretrained universal machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) via energy probing, and show this gap can be closed by a simple training-time alignment. We propose Crystal REPresentation Alignment (CrystalREPA), a plug-and-play framework that aligns the atom-wise hidden states of generative encoders with frozen MLIP representations through an element-aware contrastive objective, transferring stability-aware atomistic priors with marginal training overhead and no additional inference cost. Across three generative frameworks, ten MLIP teachers, and two benchmark datasets, CrystalREPA consistently improves the thermodynamic stability, structural validity, and structural fidelity of generated crystals. Equally important, we find that an MLIP's transfer effectiveness is poorly predicted by its accuracy on standard leaderboards (e.g., Matbench Discovery) but strongly predicted by the distinguishability of its atom-wise representation space, yielding a practical, accuracy-independent criterion for selecting MLIP teachers for generative transfer. papers.title: Distilling neural networks into equations to predict planetary instability
papers.summary: The problem of predicting when a multi-planet system will become dynamically unstable has defied analytical progress over the past three hundred years. Recent machine learning advances achieve high predictive performance of instability dynamics, but as black-box systems cannot be interpreted to connect to existing scientific understanding. Here we show analytic equations that predict when a multi-planet system will undergo instability. We discover these equations by first training a neural network on a dataset of N-body simulations, and then distilling its latent knowledge into closed-form algebraic expressions. Our two-stage pipeline first learns an interpretable variable basis, then searches for equations using symbolic regression. The resulting equations outperform existing analytic estimates of instability and apply across wide ranges of mass ratios, spacing, and orbital eccentricities. They capture structure in the prediction landscape with a small number of variables amenable to dynamical interpretation. These results demonstrate how symbolic learning can be combined with neural networks to extract scientific insight from complex dynamical systems.

papers.title: Depth Improves Training-Time Scaling for Difficult Tasks in Deep Linear Networks
papers.summary: Neural scaling laws describe the predictable power-law dependence of model performance on training time, dataset size, and model scale, with the exponents quantifying how performance changes with resources. Recent theory has shown how scaling exponents are shaped by the data distribution and the structure of the learning task, but whether network depth can improve training-time scaling has remained unsettled. Through a refined analysis of deep linear networks, we clarify that the task spectrum determines when increasing network depth improves training-time scaling. For spectrally difficult tasks, increasing depth improves the asymptotic training-time scaling exponent, whereas for easy tasks, the exponent remains independent of depth, with depth affecting only a logarithmic correction at the boundary between these regimes. Remarkably, we find that a reparameterization of time governed by the predictor norm provides a unified description of the dynamics across task difficulties. Under this reparameterization, the loss follows a common scaling law whose exponent is independent of depth. Numerical experiments on a task derived from benchmark image data and with nonlinear networks exhibit qualitatively consistent task-dependent effects of depth on training-time scaling. Our findings advance the theoretical understanding of how task structure shapes the effects of network architecture on learning and offer a basis for studying scaling behavior across broader classes of neural networks.

papers.title: Amplify, Locate, Estimate (ALE) on Rare-Failure Rates of Fine-Tuned LLMs

papers.title: Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings
papers.summary: Machine learning is widely regarded as a promising application in which quantum computing could offer a computational advantage. However, general quantum machine learning models with provable guarantees on performance, trainability, and efficient inference remain limited. In this work, we introduce quantum Hamiltonian embeddings, a supervised learning framework in which a classical training dataset is encoded into a single effective, parameterized Hamiltonian. Training optimizes the parameters of this data-dependent Hamiltonian, whose approximate ground state defines the classification rule. Once the ground state has been approximated using a quantum algorithm, inference can be performed either classically using a classical representation of the learned state, or with a quantum representation of the state. We establish efficient methods for gradient estimation and prove favorable generalization guarantees. Furthermore, under standard cryptographic assumptions, we show that Hamiltonian embeddings can realize hypothesis functions beyond the reach of efficient classical algorithms. We then demonstrate the framework at scale on IBM Heron processors using a standard benchmark dataset. Together, these results establish Hamiltonian embeddings as a new framework for quantum machine learning, combining theoretical guarantees with a path for experimental investigations at scale on quantum hardware.

papers.title: Inference Latency-Aware Tsetlin Machine Training
papers.summary: The Tsetlin Machine (TM) is a logic-based machine learning model well suited to low-latency inference on resource-constrained edge devices. Because each clause is an AND over Boolean literals, both the literals and their associated Tsetlin Automaton (TA) actions can be represented at the bit level, enabling bitwise evaluation and an early exit that is triggered as soon as any included literal evaluates to zero, forcing the clause output to zero. In this work, we study how the two TM training hyperparameters, T and s, govern both classification accuracy and inference latency. Building on the inversely proportional T-s relationship along which accuracy is nearly constant, we find that inference latency is reduced primarily by increasing s; rather than exhaustively searching the (T, s) grid at high training cost, we propose a directed search strategy that treats accuracy as a constraint and advances toward larger s to reduce inference latency within a fixed evaluation budget. Experimental results on the gem5 simulator with an ARM processor show that, for certain datasets, the search is able to increase s while preserving the baseline accuracy, thereby reducing inference latency at negligible accuracy cost: across six datasets, the method reduces inference latency by up to 16.34%, while some datasets exhibit an accuracy reduction of only 0.06%. The proposed strategy requires far fewer configuration evaluations than an exhaustive grid search.

papers.title: NOMAD-EEG: Native Omni-Montage Adaptive Diffusion
papers.summary: Purpose. Electroencephalography (EEG) montages, channel counts and recording lengths vary widely, but most EEG foundation models are bound to the channel set and input length they were trained on. We aimed to build a generative EEG foundation model independent of the number, identity and order of electrodes and of the input length. Methods. NOMAD-EEG is a 12.0 M-parameter diffusion model that alternates state-space layers along time, without patches, with attention across electrodes identified only by their 3D scalp position. It was pre-trained on 147 h of unlabelled EEG from a single corpus and evaluated with frozen linear probes on ten datasets with 1 to 64 electrodes against seven foundation models run under one protocol, and on two unseen populations. Results. Despite its small size (12.0 M parameters against 69 M for REVE) and single pre- training corpus, NOMAD-EEG outperformed all seven foundation models on EEGMMIDB mo- tor imagery (balanced accuracy 0.442), Siena seizure detection (macro F1 0.622) and Bonn seizure detection (AUROC 0.999), had the highest accuracy of the seven compared models on TUEP epilepsy diagnosis (0.640) and, after fine-tuning, the highest \k{appa} (0.635) and weighted F1 (0.814) on TUEV event classification. It was the best of five models on P300 detection in autism with an unseen eight-electrode montage (AUROC 0.718). With only 5 of 19 electrodes, its mean AUROC fell only from 0.942 to 0.891. Conclusion. Identifying electrodes by position and modelling time without patches let one small model, pre-trained on one corpus, outperform much larger EEG foundation models on seizure detection, epileptiform event classification, epilepsy diagnosis and motor imagery.

papers.title: LEAP: a Latent Embedding Anomaly Patch-Transformer for time-series anomaly detection
papers.summary: Time-series anomaly detection is dominated by reconstruction-based neural detectors, whose objective is structurally flawed. Since the target is also the input, an expressive model can learn to reconstruct anomalies too, leaving uninformative residuals. Recent large-scale benchmarks show that, on curated data, elaborate deep detectors rarely beat simple statistical baselines, while current leaders rely on representation learning. We propose LEAP (Latent Embedding Anomaly Patch-Transformer), which combines masked prediction with latent representation-based anomaly evidence, without relying on reconstruction or attention-based scoring. The model removes patches from a window and predicts them from the remaining temporal and cross-channel context, so prediction errors measure how well learned dynamics explain hidden segments. Deterministic complementary group masking ensures every time step is scored while hidden, with identical visible fractions during training and inference. LEAP adds three label-free evidence sources: latent-embedding novelty calibrated by local density, local temporal contrast, and per-channel novelty pooled over channels selected by six label-free criteria. Under the TSB-AD protocol, the full model achieves a VUS-PR of $0.5179 \pm 0.0022$ on $180$ held-out multivariate series. On TSB-AD-U, a univariate variant combining multi-scale masked-prediction scoring with latent novelty, without contrast or channel-pool novelty, achieves $0.6194 \pm 0.0016$ on $350$ held-out series. Both results average three random seeds. A five-stage ablation on TSB-AD-M, supported by paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, shows statistically significant gains from each successive component.

papers.title: Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments
papers.summary: Scaling coding agents requires a continuing supply of executable data for training, benchmarking, and continuous evaluation. Each task must couple a realistic software state with a specification, development tools, and reliable verification. To expand this supply, we present Change2Task, a system grounded in repository history that converts merged pull requests (PRs) into verified tasks on healthy modern revisions of the same repository. It aligns historical evidence with evolved code, reconstructs task states through Patch Reversal, Code Mapping, or Agent Reconstruction, and validates the lifecycle from a healthy base to a task state and a restored state. By deriving multiple tasks grounded in developer evidence from maintained environments, Change2Task provides executable data for coding agent training and evaluation while reducing repeated environment setup, storage, and task construction effort. We evaluate five coding agent task families: Bug Fix, Feature Addition, Test Generation, Application Programming Interface (API) Migration, and Security Repair. Starting from 1,130 source changes eligible for construction, Change2Task achieves 79.6% verified task construction success across these task families. On a matched candidate set, it recovers 29.2% more verified tasks than a construction baseline based on PRs. Historical and reconstructed cases achieve 89.7% aggregate matched outcome agreement under agent evaluation, while reuse of modern bases reduces measured expenditure across the complete pipeline by 10.8%. Four matched studies examine construction stages, semantic review, branch consistency, and resource trade-offs. An industrial deployment further constructs 1,000 tasks from private PR histories and evaluates four models on a fixed 500-task cohort.

papers.title: Beyond Perturbation Magnitude: Direction-Dependent Responses in Multimodal Geometric Representations
papers.summary: Geometric alignment scores based on Gram determinants provide a compact way to model higher-order consistency among modalities, yet how such scores respond to modality degradation is poorly understood. This paper asks whether the response of a multimodal geometric score is determined primarily by the magnitude of the perturbation-induced displacement. Using frozen cohorts from MSR-VTT (N=878) and DiDeMo (N=980), we apply controlled video blur and audio noise and analyze the response in the relational geometry on which the score is defined. Displacement magnitude explains at most 15% of the out-of-sample variance in the absolute response, and magnitude-matched pairs respond systematically differently, so scalar magnitude does not organize the response. The closed-form first-order expansion of the Gramian volume yields the Directional Geometric Response (DGR): the projection of the displacement onto the local volume gradient, which jointly captures the clean operating point, displacement magnitude, and displacement direction. The absolute first-order DGR term explains the observed response with out-of-sample R^2 of 0.838-0.969, matched-magnitude ranking accuracies of 0.864-0.963, and response-sign accuracies of 0.909-0.989, whereas the tested direction-free alternatives remain weak or unstable under the corresponding evaluation protocols. A pre-specified gain-normalization candidate, V/(g_V+eps), fails its predictability and clean-order gates. DGR uses the observed degraded-state displacement and is therefore an explanatory quantity, not a deployment-time predictor: geometric response depends on where the representation operates, how far degradation moves the relational geometry, and in which direction it moves.

papers.title: A Machine Learning API for Earth Observation Data Cubes Based on openEO
papers.summary: Earth Observation (EO) data are increasingly organized as spatio-temporal data cubes, while machine learning (ML) methods operate on tabular feature matrices or structured tensor inputs. This mismatch forces platform-specific transformations that are difficult to reproduce or transfer across cloud infrastructures. The openEO specification provides a unified interface for EO data access and processing across heterogeneous backends, but lacks a standardized approach for ML integration. We propose a process-level ML specification for openEO structured into three stages: model initialization, model actions (training, tuning, inference, validation), and model management. It supports classical algorithms such as Random Forest and SVM, as well as deep learning architectures for time-series and spatial patch-based modeling, including TempCNN, Temporal Attention Encoders, and foundation model inference. Three prototype implementations in R and Python demonstrate feasibility across diverse technology stacks. A crop type mapping use case demonstrates cross-backend interoperability by submitting an identical process graph to independent R and Python backends and comparing predictions and evaluation metrics. Two further use cases demonstrate deep learning on time series and foundation model inference, each executed on a dedicated backend. The prototypes reveal, however, that full cross-backend portability requires deeper harmonization of serialization formats and execution semantics than the process level alone can enforce; backend library versions and preprocessing conventions outside the specification's boundary also affect reproducibility. Addressing both through explicit backend conformance profiles represents the most important near-term direction. The specification advances the reproducibility, portability, and accessibility of ML workflows on EO data cubes across cloud platforms.

papers.title: Local Search with Correlated Randomness
papers.summary: The running-time distribution of a randomized algorithm is computed under independent randomness, but independence is rarely what a source guarantees. We study sources $ν$ satisfying $ν[w]\le DP[w]^s$ for every finite prefix $w$ of the random tape, where $P$ is an independent reference law, $0<s\le1$, and $D\ge1$; individual choices may be predictable, even determined by the past. The worst-case probability of any closed tape event $E$ is exactly $\min\{1,DC_s(E)\}$, where $C_s(E)$ is the infimum cost of covering $E$ by prefixes of varying depth, a tree max-flow/min-cut identity that makes worst-case survival probabilities exact and optimizable over the algorithm's choices. Three applications follow. For $n$ tasks on one machine, each retried until the next random symbol lies in its success set, every schedule has the same makespan distribution under independent randomness, yet under our constraint two fixed orders miss a linear deadline with worst-case probabilities $1$ and $\exp[-Θ(n)]$; a static priority rule is optimal at every deadline. For the standard local walk on a $k$-CNF with an assignment that satisfies a majority of each clause, we determine the sharp source threshold $s_*$. Below $s_*$, on some instances a single admissible source forces nontermination however clauses are selected; at $s_*$, with fixed $D$, the expected number of flips is at most cubic in the initial Hamming distance, against linear under independence, with matching worst-case instances; and any fixed margin above $s_*$ restores linear dependence on the distance. Third, verified backtracking for noisy predecessor search remains correct under a sufficiently strong bound on the comparison errors. In every setting the algorithm may also restart, which supplies no fresh randomness; restarting restores exponential tails exactly when the nontermination event has a prefix cover of cost below one.

papers.title: Adaptive Memory Index Evolution for Agents
papers.summary: Long-horizon agents continually accumulate experience, yet retaining a memory does not guarantee access when it is needed. Existing systems can adapt both memory content and access; we isolate persistent access updates as a separately controlled adaptation layer. We formulate this target as Memory Index Evolution and instantiate it with Adaptive Memory Index Evolution (AMIE), a lightweight plug-in layer that evolves per-memory access state from deployment retrievals without modifying stored content or retraining the host memory system. AMIE distils a semantic teacher's keep/suppress judgments into a retrieval-conditioned policy and accumulates its selective actions into bounded state that reweights subsequent host retrievals. Surprisingly, even a zero-call policy that simply accumulates retrieval frequency can match or outperform semantic policies in several settings, revealing retrieval traffic itself as a strong signal for access adaptation, while learned selectivity improves robustness when frequently retrieved memories remain useful. Across five retrieval-based hosts and three benchmarks, trained AMIE improves downstream F1 or accuracy in all 15 comparisons, by 0.70--3.37 percentage points (up to 25% relative), and improves retrieval in all 10 comparisons. Controlled analyses show that persistent competitor suppression can expose previously unseen evidence, while suppressing repeatedly useful memories creates the complementary failure mode. Together, these results establish persistent memory access as a practical adaptation layer, distinct from the content it serves, in retrieval-based agent memory systems.

papers.title: A Graph-informed Kriging model for sample-efficient Bayesian optimization of wind farm layouts
papers.summary: Wind farm layout optimization becomes increasingly difficult as turbine count grows, especially when high-fidelity aerodynamic models are used. Conventional Kriging-based Bayesian optimization often suffers from low sample efficiency in high-dimensional layout spaces because sparse training data provide limited domain coverage. We develop a Graph-informed Kriging framework that embeds reusable aerodynamic interaction information into the surrogate mean function. The wind farm is represented as a directed aerodynamic graph, where pairwise turbine interactions defined in a low-dimensional relative-coordinate space are assembled into a farm-scale mean. This structured mean captures the dominant variation in annual energy production (AEP), allowing the Gaussian process to model only the residual structure and uncertainty. Numerical experiments show that Graph-informed Kriging consistently improves AEP prediction accuracy over ordinary and generic-trend Kriging under sparse-data conditions, with increasing benefits as layout dimension and wake-interaction strength grow. Embedded in Bayesian optimization, it substantially improves sample efficiency and achieves competitive solutions for the IEA Wind Task 37 benchmark with about 280 AEP evaluations. In a controlled 16-turbine case, it also outperforms ordinary and multi-fidelity Kriging under the same high-fidelity evaluation budget. The framework is further extended to a 48-turbine wind farm, demonstrating applicability to large-scale CFD-based layout optimization. These results show that Graph-informed surrogate modeling can enable more efficient use of high-fidelity aerodynamic models for reliable large-scale wind farm layout design.

papers.title: Unified Approach for Weakly Supervised Multicalibration
papers.summary: Multicalibration requires predicted scores to agree with label probabilities across rich families of subgroups and score-dependent tests, but existing methods require clean input-label pairs for evaluation and post-processing. This assumption fails in weakly supervised learning (WSL) regimes -- including positive-unlabeled, unlabeled-unlabeled, and positive-confidence learning -- where clean labels are costly or unavailable even though reliable uncertainty estimates may be crucial. We address this gap by developing estimators of multicalibration error and post-hoc correction methods for WSL settings in which clean input-label pairs are unavailable. We propose a unified framework for estimating and correcting multicalibration under weak supervision by combining contamination-matrix risk rewrites with witness-based calibration constraints, yielding corrected multicalibration moments with finite-sample guarantees. We further propose weak-label multicalibration boost (WLMC), a generic post-hoc recalibration algorithm under weak supervision. Finally, we conduct experiments across multiple weak-supervision settings to evaluate multicalibration behavior and offer empirical insight into uncertainty estimation under weak supervision.

papers.title: A Hierarchical Method for Environmental Sounds Recognition in Complex Acoustic Scenes
papers.summary: Environmental noise identification is essential for noise control, yet conventional single-stage classifiers suffer from class confusion under imbalanced multiclass conditions. This paper proposes a lightweight hierarchical model integrating a Frequency-Time Adaptive Network (FTANet) with a two-stage classification mechanism. In the first stage, FTANet classifies sounds into five coarse-grained categories covering 25 fine-grained classes. On a self-constructed dataset, FTANet achieves 95.45% coarse-grained accuracy with only 0.2004M parameters. On UrbanSound8K, it achieves 79.24% mean accuracy and 80.37% mean F1-score in ten-fold evaluation, outperforming compared convolutional models. Field tests on the Tianjin Online Acoustic Environment Monitoring Platform yield 87.94% coarse-grained accuracy and 97.21% conditional fine-grained accuracy for natural sounds correctly routed to C2. papers.title: SymADiT: Symmetry-Aware Crystal Generation with Latent Flow Matching

papers.title: Parity-equivariant prediction of conformer-resolved electronic circular dichroism spectra accelerates absolute configuration assignment
papers.summary: Electronic circular dichroism (ECD) is a key experimental probe for assigning the absolute configuration of chiral molecules, but interpreting measured spectra often requires costly time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) calculations. papers.title: Probabilistic adjustment of seasonal forecasts using cVAE with a non-parametric decoder: A case study of Arctic sea ice predictions
papers.summary: Seasonal climate predictions support planning and risk management by offering early information of the likely climate conditions in the coming months, and associated uncertainties. Ensemble forecasts enable this by simulating many plausible outcomes, allowing predictions to be expressed as usable probabilities. Large ensembles and high-resolution forecasts strengthen this by better sampling uncertainty and capturing finer-scale processes but come with significant computational cost. Moreover, forecast ensembles drift and exhibit systematic biases and spatio-temporal errors that grow with lead time, requiring careful post-processing and calibration. A probabilistic post-processing framework based on conditional Variational Autoencoders (cVAEs) was developed at the Canadian Center for Climate Modeling and Analysis to generate large ensembles of adjusted seasonal predictions of Arctic sea ice. The generative model was designed to learn the observational distribution conditioned on the biased model prediction. This enables generation of arbitrarily large ensembles of calibrated, bias corrected forecasts with improved skill. Here, we extend this framework to a Generalized Variational Inference problem to address the loss of fine-scale energy and the characteristic blurriness, a known limitation of standard cVAEs. Specifically, we employ a generator in place of the Gaussian parametrized decoder in cVAE and use Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) in the objective function instead of the Gaussian log-likelihood. We further use a higher resolution target dataset compared to the raw forecast. We show that the adjusted forecasts are better calibrated, more consistent with the observational distribution, and exhibit smaller errors than benchmark predictions, while also enhancing the resolution of the raw forecasts and improving sharpness and spectral power relative to the standard cVAE.

papers.title: When Respondents Are Scarce: LLM-Derived Semantic Priors for Bayesian Confirmatory Factor Analysis
papers.summary: Across social and behavioral research, measuring latent constructs can be challenging when target populations are small or difficult to reach. Recruiting additional respondents may be costly or infeasible, leaving researchers with limited data for estimating questionnaire factor structures. Yet item wording contains structural expectations before data collection, and whether these can improve small-sample estimation without replacing empirical validation remains unclear. We introduce the Semantic-Empirical Updating Framework (SEUF), which converts large language model paraphrases and embeddings, aligned with hypothesized item-factor assignments, into prespecified priors for Bayesian confirmatory factor analysis. We evaluated SEUF using a 38-item survey of 617 industrial-park stakeholders and two public surveys, FEVS and RIASEC. Semantic structure persisted after wording controls across all three instruments. With 50 respondents, SEUF achieved loading precision comparable to conventional CFA with 70-82 respondents, equivalent to 29-39% fewer respondents at the specified precision benchmark. Results showed lower loading errors and improved credible-interval coverage relative to conventional CFA in both public surveys. Gains were greatest when respondent data were limited, highlighting the value of semantic priors under information scarcity. By harnessing structural information already embedded in questionnaires, SEUF advances a more resource-efficient approach to measurement and opens new directions for study design and empirical inference in hard-to-reach populations.

papers.title: Interpretable Brain Age Prediction Using White Matter Fiber Orientation Distributions with Rotation-Equivariant Deep Learning
papers.summary: Diffusion MRI (dMRI) provides information about white matter microstructure that can support brain age prediction. Averaging predictions from five cross-validation models yielded a mean absolute error of 3.54 years and Pearson's correlation of 0.958. Our results indicated that the performance advantage depended on combining WM-FODs with equivariant processing. Prediction accuracy was highest at a maximum SH order of Lmax = 2 and declined at higher orders. These findings support rotation-equivariant processing of WM-FODs for accurate brain age prediction with anatomically interpretable model sensitivity.

papers.title: TimeWorld: Towards Action-Conditioned Multimodal World Models for Time Series Forecasting
papers.summary: Time series forecasting supports decision-making in web applications such as online retail and network management, where planned actions can reshape future dynamics. World models provide a natural paradigm for predicting such action-dependent changes beyond extrapolating historical patterns. However, existing time series world models (TSWMs) typically rely on fixed, domain-specific covariate schemas that limit flexible intervention specification, while multimodal forecasters treat text primarily as passive predictive context. To investigate these gaps, we introduce TSWM-Bench, a cross-domain benchmark for multimodal TSWMs spanning seven real-world datasets, with textual interventions grounded in recorded action--outcome data. Our evaluation reveals that conventional multimodal forecasters underperform history-only time series foundation models (TSFMs) despite dataset-specific training, whereas simple text-prefix adaptations improve forecasting across all evaluated TSFM backbones. These findings suggest that pretrained TSFMs encode implicit world knowledge of temporal dynamics, offering a strong foundation for action-conditioned modeling beyond conventional multimodal fusion. Building on this insight, we propose TimeWorld, a plug-in framework that adapts pretrained TSFMs through explicit action-response modeling. Specifically, the Prototype-Guided Latent Modulation (PLM) module grounds textual actions in temporal dynamics by composing representative response prototypes to modulate future representations based on the action and historical patterns. The Action Contrastive Learning (ACL) component strengthens action-specific response modeling by contrasting these updates under alternative interventions sharing the same history, distinguishing action types while preserving relative intensity relationships.

papers.title: Mechanistic Insights into LoRA: Layer Sparsity for Adaptive Fine-Tuning via Path Patching

papers.title: Differentiable FEM versus PINN for pavement layer inverse analysis: enforcing physics as hard or soft constraints
papers.summary: Automatic-differentiation-based inverse analysis methods, including physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and differentiable programming, have recently shown great promise due to their ability to compute accurate gradients and convergence efficiency. However, their applicability to falling weight deflectometer (FWD) backcalculation remains unexplored. This study critically evaluates PINN-based inverse analysis for a multilayer pavement system and investigates differentiable finite element method (DiffFEM) as an alternative based on a synthetic benchmark. The standard PINN does not recover layer moduli because of the sharp domain discontinuities inherent to layered pavement systems. Although we use an extended PINN with domain decomposition (XPINN), which shows better performance on discontinuous domains, its performance remains highly sensitive to loss weighting and network architecture, and degrades under measurement noise. By contrast, DiffFEM consistently achieves more accurate, stable, and computationally efficient inversion results. These results show and quantify the expected advantage of DiffFEM, which enforces the governing physics as a hard constraint in the solver, over PINN-based approaches, where the governing physics is imposed as a soft constraint through the loss function. More broadly, the findings suggest that the choice between PINN- and DiffFEM-based inverse analysis needs careful consideration, with DiffFEM offering practical advantages when an efficient and robust differentiable forward solver is available.

papers.title: Investigating and Alleviating Harm Amplification in LLM Interactions
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can serve as helpful assistants, yet they can equally function as harm amplifiers that enable malicious users to achieve harmful outcomes beyond their capabilities through extended interactions. This risk manifests along two axes, i.e., democratizing domain expertise that allows novices to produce specialized harmful content, and scaling harmful operations at volumes that manual effort cannot match. Existing works, however, often overlook how LLMs compound harm across multi-turn conversations. We introduce HarmAmp, a new benchmark for multi-turn harm amplification scenarios spanning twelve risk categories. Each scenario is grounded in real-world threats and satisfies rigorous criteria, i.e., substantive amplification, operational specificity, and multi-turn necessity. We further propose TrajSafe, a proactive monitor that anticipates harmful trajectories and intervenes through actions such as probing users' genuine intents and steering the models towards safer completion. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that TrajSafe significantly reduces the harmfulness incurred in multi-turn interactions while preserving a low over-refusal rate and the target model's general capabilities. Our work offers a promising paradigm to alleviate the nuanced safety risks in LLM interactions.

papers.summary: Language-Only Vision-Language Model Selection (LOVM) aims to identify the Vision-Language Model (VLM) with the highest zero-shot accuracy on a target task using only textual information. papers.title: When Momentum Helps Polyak--Ruppert Averaging

papers.title: Sparse Sum-of-Squares Layers for Certified Learning
papers.summary: A central limitation of modern machine learning systems is the lack of formal certificates guaranteeing their behavior beyond empirical, sample-based evaluation. papers.title: MARLIN: De Novo Molecular Structure Elucidation from Tandem Mass Spectra without a Ground-Truth Formula

papers.title: Data-driven Discovery of Lie Symmetries and First Integrals with Latent ODEs

papers.title: Winner's Curse Drives False Promises in Data-Driven Decisions
papers.summary: A major challenge in data-driven decision-making is accurate policy evaluation---i.e., guaranteeing that a learned decision-making policy achieves the promised benefits. A popular strategy is model-based policy evaluation, which estimates a model from data to infer counterfactual outcomes. This strategy is known to produce unwarrantedly optimistic estimates of the true benefit due to the winner's curse. We searched the recent literature on data-driven decision-making, identifying a sample of 55 papers published in Management Science in the past decade; all but two relied on this flawed methodology. Several common justifications are provided: (1) the estimated models are accurate, stable, and well-calibrated, (2) the historical data uses random treatment assignment, (3) the model family is well-specified, and (4) the evaluation methodology uses sample splitting. Unfortunately, we show that no combination of these justifications avoids the winner's curse. First, we provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that the winner's curse can cause large, spurious reported benefits even when all these justifications hold. Second, we perform a simulation study based on the recent and consequential data-driven refugee matching problem. We construct a synthetic refugee matching environment (calibrated to closely match the real setting) but designed so that no assignment policy can improve expected employment compared to random assignment. Model-based methods report large, stable gains of around 60% even when the true effect is zero; these gains are on par with improvements of 22-75% reported in the literature. Our results provide strong evidence against model-based evaluation.

papers.title: Synthetic Data Augmentation for Functional Data: Wasserstein Risk Bounds and Diffusion-Based Conditional Generation
papers.summary: Functional data are costly to collect; samples of tens to hundreds of curves are common. Synthetic data augmentation can help, but its theory is developed for finite-dimensional data and relies on total variation, which is uninformative for functions. We study augmentation with a class-conditional functional diffusion generator and state guarantees in the Wasserstein-1 distance. For stable downstream estimators, we bound the risk of training on synthetic curves, from above and below, by the risk of training on as many real curves plus a generation penalty, and derive the best number of synthetic curves and a condition under which synthetic data outperform real data. For allocating synthetic curves under class imbalance, we bound the excess risk of training on real and synthetic curves together, without sample splitting. In applications to temperature, hyperspectral and gait curves, augmentation improved classification, function-to-scalar regression and function-to-function regression, and directing synthetic curves to the minority class gave the largest gain under class imbalance.

papers.title: Exponential Wake-Up Overshoot in Explicit Gaussian Point-Process Filters
papers.summary: When events resume after a long silence, explicit Gaussian point-process filters amplify the first update exponentially in the silence duration. We give the exact distribution of this update and a computable index that predicts when it overshoots. For the explicit (single-scoring-step) filter and its implicit posterior-mode counterpart, we derive second-order silence expansions of the state variance with opposite-sign logarithmic corrections. The crossing index determines when the post-wake prediction exceeds the resumed rate, separating the bin width at which the amplification exponent reaches one from the larger width at which the true rate is overshot. At fixed bin width, the implicit filter's expected loss grows logarithmically with silence duration, whereas a continuous-time counterexample rules out a bound uniform in bin width and silence duration. Experimental evaluation confirms these predictions in all 73 crossing cells and on exchange trade data, while variance caps reduce explicit overshoot but mostly hurt the implicit filter.

papers.title: When Does Cheap Physics Help? Gated Multi-Fidelity Physics-Informed Networks with Provable Sample Savings and Conformal Guarantees
papers.summary: High-fidelity (HF) simulations of parametric partial differential equations are expensive, whereas low-fidelity (LF) models such as coarse grids or simplified physics are cheap but biased. Multi-fidelity physics-informed neural networks combine the two, yet it remains unclear when cheap physics actually reduces the number of HF solves, and existing methods silently fail when the LF model is misleading and offer no guaranteed uncertainty. We answer the first question with a sharp sample-complexity bound: learning the HF field through its discrepancy from the LF model reduces the number of HF samples needed for accuracy $\varepsilon$ by the factor $κ^{2γ}$, where $κ$ is the ratio of the complexity of the discrepancy to that of the HF field and $γ$ is the effective-dimension exponent, and we confirm the predicted scaling with exact risk computations in a kernel model. Guided by the analysis, we propose GaMF-PINN, a gated multi-fidelity PINN that learns where to trust the LF model and falls back to physics-only learning where it does not, together with a function-level conformal procedure that returns uncertainty bands containing the entire HF solution with probability at least $1-α$ in finite samples. We release MFPDE-Bench, an open benchmark of paired LF/HF solvers for four parametric PDEs with coarse-grid and simplified-physics LF models. Across MFPDE-Bench, GaMF-PINN reaches the accuracy of a standard HF-PINN with up to 8x fewer HF solves, remains robust when the LF model is deliberately corrupted, and attains the nominal coverage where Bayesian PINNs and deep ensembles under-cover.

papers.title: TCSP3.0: Template-Based Crystal Structure Prediction with Coefficient-Preserving Element Substitution and Structural Diversity
papers.summary: Template-based crystal structure prediction (CSP) transfers a known crystal structure to a new composition by element substitution, so its accuracy depends on retrieving suitable templates, mapping elements and ranking the resulting candidates correctly. Auditing the original TCSP2.0 implementation on the T180 benchmark, we found that 469 of its 2,347 selected structures (20%) have the wrong composition, caused by element mappings that ignore stoichiometric coefficients and by sequential text substitution that cascades or corrupts element symbols. We propose TCSP3.0, which enforces coefficient-preserving mappings, substitutes species simultaneously on parsed structures and validates every candidate's composition and cell. It further adds periodic-number retrieval, soft oxidation-state evidence, radius-compatibility scoring, structural deduplication, and ORB-v3 machine-learning-potential relaxation and energy ranking of its candidates, as used by deep generative CSP baselines. TCSP3.0 achieves Top-1 and Top-20 match rates of 72.2% and 90.6% on T180, compared with 28.3% and 45.6% for TCSP2.0, and a Top-20 match rate of 74.0% on a new 800-target benchmark (T800). On T180 it also outperforms PNcsp+ and deep generative models CrystalFlow and MaskGXT (Top-1 72.2% versus at most 63.9%). Even without relaxation, TCSP3.0 reaches 67.8% at Top-1 and 90.6% at Top-20 in a median of 28 s per target on two CPU cores, about ten times faster than CrystalFlow. Paired ten-arm ablations on T180 and T800 show that most of the improvement comes from the correctness fixes; structural deduplication significantly improves the Top-5 match rate, embedding-based retrieval is required for coverage, and the remaining scoring features have small or null effects.
